title: Weekly vs Monthly Sensex Options: Why the Same Strike Has Two Prices
summary: The same Sensex 82,500 call cost ₹377 on the weekly expiry and ₹703 on the monthly at the same moment. Learn why one strike has two prices.
body_markdown:
Weekly and monthly Sensex options at the same strike have different prices because the monthly contract has more days left to expiry. More days give Sensex more time to move, so buyers pay more for the monthly option.


At 9:16 am on 17 Nov, the Sensex 82,500 call cost ₹377.05 on the 19 Nov weekly expiry and ₹703.05 on the 26 Nov monthly expiry. For one lot of 20 units, that is ₹7,541 against ₹14,061.

## What Are Weekly and Monthly Sensex Options?


A Sensex option is a contract on BSE’s Sensex index. A call gains when Sensex rises above a chosen level, called the strike. A put gains when Sensex falls below it. Every option has an expiry date, after which it stops trading.


-


Sensex weekly options[expire every Thursday](https://algotest.in/blog/sensex-expiry-day/) .


-


The monthly contract expires on the last Thursday of the month.


-


If that Thursday is a trading holiday, expiry moves to the previous trading day.


-


In the last week of the month, the nearest expiry is the monthly contract itself.


Each expiry has its own price for every strike. On the[Sensex option chain](https://algotest.in/sensex-option-chain) on[AlgoTest](https://algotest.in/) , every expiry tab shows a different premium for the same strike. The premium is the price you pay for one unit of the option.


Sensex options trade in lots of[20 units](https://algotest.in/blog/sensex-lot-size/) , so one lot costs 20 times the premium. For contracts expiring in January 2027 and later, the lot size becomes 25.

## Why Does the Monthly Option Cost More?


An option’s price has two parts. Intrinsic value is what the option would be worth if it expired right now.[Time value](https://algotest.in/blog/black-scholes-option-pricing-model/) is the extra amount buyers pay for the chance that Sensex moves further before expiry.


-


The monthly had 9 days left and the weekly had 2, so monthly buyers paid for 7 more days in which Sensex could move.


-


The 82,500 call was[out of the money](https://algotest.in/blog/itm-atm-otm/) , which means it had no intrinsic value. Its whole price was time value.


-


The 82,500 put was ₹264.15 in the money on both expiries. Without that part, its time value was ₹319.80 on the weekly and ₹610.05 on the monthly.


-


Price does not grow in a straight line with days. The monthly had 4.5 times the days left but cost only about 1.9 times as much.


-


The weekly had the higher[implied volatility (IV)](https://algotest.in/blog/implied-volatility-and-how-to-read-and-compute-iv/) , 18.3 against 15.1. IV shows how big a move the market is pricing in. The weekly was still cheaper because it had far less time.


## How Fast Does Each Expiry Lose Value?


Theta is how much an option’s price falls in one day if nothing else changes. Vega is how much the price changes when IV moves by one point. Both are[option Greeks](https://algotest.in/blog/option-greeks/) , and the Simulator shows them for every position.


-


The weekly put was losing about ₹2,056 a day per lot.


-


The monthly put was losing about ₹850 a day per lot.


-


The weekly was losing value about 2.4 times as fast, even though it cost less.


-


The monthly reacted more to IV. Its vega was about ₹1,043 per lot, against ₹510 for the weekly.


A weekly buyer pays less but has to be right quickly. A monthly buyer pays more for time, and a change in IV moves that price more.


## How Much More Does One Lot Cost?


For one lot of 20, the weekly 82,500 call cost ₹7,541 and the monthly call cost ₹14,061. The monthly cost ₹6,520 more for the same strike, and in return the trade had 7 more days to work.


On the put side, the gap was ₹5,805: ₹11,679 for the weekly against ₹17,484 for the monthly.


The higher price also moves the breakeven, which is the Sensex level at expiry where a buyer neither gains nor loses. The weekly call broke even at 82,877, which is 641 points above spot. The monthly call needed 83,203, which is 967 points above spot, but it had 9 days to get there instead of 2.

## Which Expiry Fits Your Trade?


Neither expiry is better in every case. The right one depends on how much time your view needs.


-


A weekly fits a view that should play out within a day or two, because it costs less and you need little time.


-


A monthly fits a view that may take a week or more, because it loses less each day while you wait.


-


If your trade depends on an event like an[RBI policy day](https://algotest.in/blog/rbi-policy-and-fed-dates/) , check whether the event falls before or after the weekly expiry.


-


Option sellers face the reverse trade-off. Faster decay on the weekly works in their favour, but a sharp move close to expiry can hurt them more.

### Choose the Expiry Before You Choose the Strike


The strike is only half of an options trade. The expiry decides how much you pay, how fast you lose value while you wait, and how long your view has to work.


Before your next Sensex trade, write down how many days your view needs. Compare the premium, daily decay and breakeven for both expiries at the same minute. Set your exit and the most you will risk per lot, then replay a few past sessions to see how each expiry behaved.

### FAQs


#### Why are monthly options more expensive than weekly options?


A monthly option has more days left, so it carries more time value. In the 82,500 example, the monthly call cost about 1.9 times the weekly call at the same minute.


#### Do weekly options lose value faster than monthly options?


Yes. Time decay speeds up as expiry gets closer, so a weekly option usually loses a bigger share of its price each day. A sharp move in Sensex can still push either option up.


#### Can a weekly option have a higher IV than a monthly option?


Yes. Near-term IV often rises when traders expect a big move soon, such as around an event. A higher IV does not make the weekly cost more than the monthly, because the monthly still has more time left.


#### Why does a weekly option need a smaller move to break even?


It costs less, so Sensex has to travel a shorter distance to cover what you paid. The catch is time: the weekly has only a few days to make that move.


#### Is a weekly or monthly Sensex option better for beginners?


Neither suits everyone. Weekly options cost less per lot but can lose value very fast, while monthly options cost more and give a view more time. Practising both on past sessions shows how each behaves before real money is involved.


#### Does every strike exist in both weekly and monthly Sensex options?


Strikes near the current Sensex level are usually listed in both. Each expiry has its own list of strikes, so check the option chain for that expiry before you plan a trade.
